title: Emerging Modes of Business
tagline: How e-business, the internet and new delivery models change the way trade is conducted. Unit weight: 5 marks.

overview.intro: The arrival of the internet did not invent new needs; it changed the cost of reaching them. Search became cheap, comparison became free, and a seller in one town could hold stock only after an order was placed. This five-mark unit covers the emerging modes of business, with e-business at its centre: what e-business is and how it differs from traditional trading, its merits and limitations, the different forms it takes from online retail to business-to-business exchanges, and the wider emerging models such as outsourcing, franchising and the subscription and platform economy that have grown alongside it.

facts.label: E-business scope
facts.value: Any business transaction or process executed over electronic networks, including buying, selling and servicing.

facts.label: Common forms
facts.value: Business to consumer, business to business, consumer to consumer, and online services such as banking and learning.

facts.label: Core limitation
facts.value: Digital divide, security and privacy risk, inability to inspect goods, and dependence on delivery and logistics.

learningOutcomes: Define e-business and distinguish it from traditional business.
State the merits and limitations of e-business.
Classify the main forms of e-business.
Describe other emerging modes such as outsourcing and franchising.
Judge when an online mode suits a product and when it does not.

learn.title: Emerging modes and the meaning of e-business

blocks.text: Emerging modes of business are the newer ways in which organisations organise, reach and serve customers, made possible largely by electronic networks. E-business, the central example, is the conduct of business processes over the internet and other electronic networks, covering not only buying and selling but also after-sales service, production coordination and internal collaboration. It differs from traditional business in that the transaction and much of the delivery are digital, the market is not limited by geography, and the cost of reaching an additional customer is very low once the platform exists.

items.note: A hybrid mode: physical presence for trust and immediacy, electronic reach for convenience.

items.text: A firm buying components from three countries through a single tender portal.
items.note: Business-to-business e-business reducing the search and paperwork cost of procurement.

learn.title: Merits, limitations and forms of e-business

blocks.text: The merits of e-business follow directly from cheap search and cheap reach: convenience for the customer who shops at any hour, a wider market without opening branches, lower operating cost since a virtual store needs no prime-location property, easy comparison of price and specification, and immediate delivery for products that can be digitised. The limitations are equally concrete: the buyer cannot inspect or try the goods, security and privacy of data remain a live risk, delivery takes days and can fail, the digital divide excludes sections of the population, and disputes are harder to resolve when the seller may be in another jurisdiction.

blocks.caption: Forms of e-business
rows: Firm selling directly to the final buyer
An online store selling books and electronics
A manufacturer sourcing components on a portal
A person selling a used phone on a marketplace
Internet banking, online learning, ticket booking

items: Merits: convenience, wider reach, lower cost, easy comparison, round-the-clock trading.
Limitations: no physical inspection, security and privacy risk, delivery dependence.
Digital divide: customers without connectivity or digital literacy are excluded.
Returns and disputes cost more when the parties are distant.
Trust must be manufactured through reviews, ratings, clear returns and secure payment.

learn.title: Other emerging modes: outsourcing, franchising and platforms

blocks.text: Beyond e-business, several newer modes have become standard. Outsourcing is the practice of taking a non-core activity out of the firm and contracting it to a specialist, which converts a fixed cost into a variable one and lets the firm concentrate on what it does best. Franchising lets an established brand expand rapidly by granting an independent operator the right to run an outlet under its system and standards. The platform model connects two or more groups of users and earns from the transaction or the visibility it facilitates, while the subscription model converts a single purchase into a recurring relationship.

blocks.caption: Emerging modes and what each achieves
rows: Buys a non-core activity from a specialist
Loss of control and dependence on the supplier
Expands through independent operators using a proven system
Connects producers and users and earns from the exchange
Quality and dispute handling between users
Converts one-off sales into recurring revenue
Churn if the value delivered falls short
Fulfils orders using a flexible network

items.text: A food brand opening outlets through franchisees.
items.note: The brand gains rapid expansion with the franchisee’s capital, while standards must be policed through the agreement.

items.text: A manufacturer outsourcing its entire customer support operation.
items.note: Cost becomes variable and specialist skill is gained, at the price of direct control over the customer experience.

learn.title: When an emerging mode suits a product

blocks.text: The mode must fit the product. Digital goods, standardised items, repeat purchases and products with reliable descriptions work well online, because inspection adds little and convenience adds much. Products whose choice depends on fit, feel, colour or freshness, and products needing installation or service, work better in a physical channel or a hybrid one. The sensible design question is not whether to go online but which parts of the customer journey should be digital and which should remain human.

items: Standardisation: a product identical across units can be sold unseen.
Value of time: convenience matters more than inspection for many categories.
Trust signals: reviews, ratings and easy returns substitute for physical examination.
Hybrid wins most cases: digital discovery and payment with physical fulfilment.
Data use must stay within the law and the customer’s reasonable expectation.

keyPoints: Emerging modes are newer ways of organising and reaching customers, chiefly through electronic networks.
E-business covers any business process run over electronic networks, not only selling.
E-business reaches a global market at a near-fixed cost of serving one more customer.
Merits: convenience, wider reach, lower cost, easy comparison, continuous trading.
Limitations: no inspection, security and privacy risk, delivery dependence, digital divide.
Forms: business to consumer, business to business, consumer to consumer, and online services.
Outsourcing converts a fixed cost into a variable one and concentrates the firm on its core work.
Franchising expands through independent operators working to a proven system.
Platform models earn by connecting parties; subscription models convert sales into recurring revenue.
The right question is which part of the journey to digitise, not whether to go online.
examFocus: Five marks rewards a crisp definition, a merits and limitations pair, and one example per form.
Comparison questions should take one basis at a time rather than describing the two separately.
In suitability answers, name the product characteristics that decide the channel.

questions.prompt: E-business differs from traditional business mainly in that:
options: Its processes and transactions run over electronic networks
It never needs delivery or logistics
It is not subject to consumer law
questions.answer: Its processes and transactions run over electronic networks
questions.explanation: E-business is defined by the electronic execution of business processes, whether or not the product itself is digital.

questions.prompt: A manufacturer buying components from suppliers through a web portal is practising:
questions.explanation: Both parties to the transaction are firms, which is the definition of business-to-business e-business.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a limitation of e-business?
options: Inability of the buyer to inspect goods before purchase
Lower operating cost than a physical store
questions.answer: Inability of the buyer to inspect goods before purchase
questions.explanation: The buyer relies on description and reviews rather than physical examination, which is why returns policies matter so much online.

questions.prompt: Converting a fixed production cost into a variable cost by giving an activity to a specialist supplier describes:
questions.explanation: The firm stops carrying the fixed cost of the function and pays for it as used, which is the financial logic of outsourcing.

questions.prompt: The exclusion of people who lack connectivity or digital skill from electronic trade is called the digital __________ .
questions.explanation: The divide describes the gap between those who can participate in digital commerce and those who cannot.

questions.prompt: A model in which a business sells access to a product or service for a recurring periodic payment is the __________ model.
questions.explanation: Subscription converts a single transaction into a recurring relationship and revenue that can be forecast.

questions.answer: Four merits are: the customer can shop at any hour without travelling; the market is not limited by geography, so even a small firm can reach a national audience; the operating cost is lower because a virtual store needs no prime-location property; and comparison of price and specification is easy for the buyer, which forces competitive pricing. Immediate delivery of digital products is also accepted.
questions.explanation: Each merit must be linked to the electronic mechanism that produces it, not merely asserted.

questions.prompt: Distinguish e-business from traditional business on three bases.
questions.answer: On market reach, e-business serves a global audience through a network while traditional business is confined largely to its locality. On cost, the cost of reaching one more customer in e-business is close to fixed once the platform exists, whereas each new traditional location adds cost. On customer information, e-business collects detail instantly at every step, while traditional business gathers it slowly and partially. The hours of trading also differ, since an online store never closes.
questions.explanation: Three bases of comparison are needed, each stated as a contrast between the two.

questions.prompt: Explain the merits and limitations of e-business.
questions.answer: The merits are convenience, since the customer can order at any hour without travelling; wider market reach, because a small seller can serve customers anywhere the delivery network reaches; lower operating cost, as no prime-location property is required; easy comparison of price, specification and reviews, which improves the buyer’s position; and speed of payment and of delivery for goods that can be digitised. The limitations are that the buyer cannot inspect or try the product before purchase, so trust must be created through ratings and returns policies; that security and privacy of customer data carry real risk; that fulfilment depends on delivery networks that can fail; that the digital divide excludes people without connectivity or skill; and that disputes are harder to resolve when the seller is in another jurisdiction. For services and standardised goods the merits dominate, while for products dependent on fit or feel the limitations can outweigh them.
questions.explanation: Full marks need at least three merits and three limitations with reasoning, plus a judgement about which products suit the mode.

questions.prompt: A local footwear maker wants to sell online. Describe the hybrid model you would recommend, the limitations that must be managed, and one metric that would show whether it is working.
questions.answer: The recommended model keeps what must be physical and digitises what need not be: a catalogue site with detailed sizing charts, photographs from several angles and customer reviews provides discovery and ordering, while the shop remains the point for trying on, fitting and returns. Payment should be available both online and at the counter, and the store can serve as a collection and return point, which converts its location from a cost into an asset. The limitations to manage are the buyer’s inability to judge fit remotely, addressed by a generous returns policy and consistent sizing data; delivery failure and delay, addressed by a named courier with tracking; and data privacy, addressed by collecting only what payment requires and stating how it is used. The metric to watch is the proportion of online orders that are returned, because a rising return rate means the sizing and description are failing, and it is a better early signal than revenue, which can rise while the model loses money on returns.
questions.explanation: The answer is marked on a concrete hybrid design, named limitations with matching controls, and a single metric justified rather than a list of many.
